ms: (a) the same music repeated for each verse
(b) new music for each section of the text (no repeated verse music)
questions.model: (a) The same music for every verse. (b) New music for each part of the text.

questions.q:
Define:
(a) a cappella
(b) mickey-mousing (in film or cartoon music)
ms: (a) singing without instrumental accompaniment
(b) music that closely mirrors the action on screen (e.g. a falling glissando when a character falls)
questions.model: (a) Singing with no instruments. (b) Music that copies the on-screen action exactly, e.g. a slide down as someone falls.

questions.q:
Suggest how a composer could set each phrase to music using word-painting or word-setting.
(a) "climbing to the mountain top"
(b) "falling tears"
(c) "whisper"
(d) "Alleluia, rejoice!"
ms: (a) a rising (ascending) melody, ending on a high note
(b) a descending melody / falling (chromatic) phrase / falling semitone 'sighs'
(c) pianissimo / very quiet, thin accompaniment
(d) a melisma / fast, decorated notes on one syllable, major key, forte
questions.model: (a) A rising melody that ends on a high, held note. (b) A descending chromatic line in a minor key. (c) Sung pianissimo over a very thin accompaniment. (d) A long, joyful melisma on 'Alleluia', forte and in a major key.

questions.q: In a film, a heroic leitmotif is heard whenever the hero appears. Later the hero is defeated. Explain four ways the composer could change the leitmotif to show this.
ms: change from major to minor key
slower tempo
quieter dynamics (piano)
thinner texture / solo instrument instead of full brass
change of instrument/timbre (e.g. solo oboe or low strings instead of trumpets)
fragment the theme / leave it unfinished (imperfect cadence)
add dissonant or chromatic harmony
questions.model: The composer could put the theme in a minor key, play it slowly and quietly, give it to a solo oboe instead of the brass, and break it off before the end so it sounds unfinished.
questions.tip: Leitmotifs are transformed, not replaced: keep the theme recognisable but change its character.

questions.q: Describe how a typical verse–chorus song from a musical, such as A Million Dreams, builds from a quiet opening to a powerful final chorus.
ms: verse–chorus structure, with a bridge / middle eight for contrast
starts quietly with a simple accompaniment (e.g. solo piano or guitar)
texture thickens: more instruments and voices added through the song
dynamics grow: crescendo to forte/fortissimo in the last chorus
the chorus uses a memorable hook / repeated melody
rising melodic shape / higher register in later choruses
possible key change (modulation up) or added harmony/backing vocals for the final chorus
rhythm section/drums enter to add drive
questions.model: The song is in verse–chorus form. It opens quietly with a soloist over a simple piano accompaniment. Each section adds instruments and voices, so the texture thickens, and the dynamics grow. The chorus has a memorable hook with a rising shape. After a contrasting bridge, the final chorus is sung fortissimo with full band and backing harmonies, possibly after a key change upwards.

questions.q: Compare music for film with music for video games.
ms: both use leitmotifs / themes for characters or places
both create atmosphere and support the action (e.g. tension, excitement)
both may use orchestral and/or electronic sounds
film: fixed length, composed to match exact timings of scenes
film: can mirror specific moments (hits, mickey-mousing)
games: built from loops that repeat seamlessly while the player explores
games: adaptive/interactive, changing with the player's actions or situation (e.g. battle music)
games: the length is unknown, so music must repeat without becoming irritating
max 4 if no similarity or no difference is given
questions.model: Both use themes for characters and places, and both create atmosphere and tension using orchestral or electronic sounds. Film music is written to a fixed length and can hit exact moments on screen. Game music is built from loops that repeat seamlessly for as long as the player explores, and it is adaptive: it changes when the action changes, for example when a battle starts.
